title: Maintaining code you did not write

sections.skill: Keep generated code understandable, documented and owned

questions.prompt: Is code read or written more often?

choices.text: Written more often, because each line of code is written many times and read only once

questions.correct_answer: Read and changed more often
questions.intro: Code is usually read and changed far more often than it is written. Generated code you cannot explain becomes a problem when it breaks or needs a change. Keep code MAINTAINABLE: clear NAMES (total_price, not x2), short FUNCTIONS that each do one thing, COMMENTS that explain why, and a README (a document explaining what the project does and how to run it). Every piece of code in use should have an OWNER: a person who understands it and is responsible for fixing it. If no one can explain how it works, it is not ready to rely on.

sections.skill: Compare maintainable code with a well-labeled kitchen

questions.prompt: Labeled jars are like what in code?

choices.text: Very short names like x and y

questions.correct_answer: Clear names and comments
questions.intro: In a shared kitchen with LABELED jars ("sugar," "salt"), anyone can cook. In a kitchen of unlabeled jars, only the person who filled them knows which is which, and when they are away, someone puts salt in the cake. Code works the same way: clear names and comments are labels. A README is the note on the fridge explaining how things work. The OWNER is the person who restocks and keeps it organized.

sections.title: Apply it

questions.prompt: Code contains 0.0825 with no explanation. What is this called?
questions.correct_answer: A magic number
questions.intro: Maintenance problems build up quietly. "Magic numbers" such as 0.0825 with no explanation leave the next person guessing (is it a tax rate?). Duplicated code means a fix in one place is missed in another. When a tool generates a large solution, ask for a simpler version, add tests that describe how it should behave, and write down any decisions. When the owner leaves a team or class, hand over the knowledge, not just the files.
